inline.s: “Good man, all bodhisattvas and all beings of the final age should depart far from every illusion-like, false, and vain realm; because of firmly holding to the mind of departure, that mind which is itself like an illusion is also to be departed from; that departure is itself an illusion, and is also to be departed from; departing from the illusion of departure is likewise to be departed from; and when one reaches the point of nothing more to depart from, all illusions are removed. It is like drilling for fire: two sticks are rubbed together, fire comes forth and the wood is consumed, the ash flies and the smoke is extinguished; using illusion to cultivate illusion is just the same—when all illusions are extinguished, one does not fall into annihilation
(it is not that everything becomes nothing; the wondrous enlightened mind shines forth in full).

“Good man! Knowing illusion, one is at once free of it, without resorting to skillful means; freed of illusion, one is at once awake, and there are no gradual stages. All bodhisattvas and all beings of the final age who practice in accord with this will thus be able forever to depart from all illusions.

“At that time the World-Honored One, wishing to proclaim this meaning again, spoke in verse: Samantabhadra, you should know, all beings without exception have, from beginningless time, illusory ignorance, all established from the Tathagatas' mind of perfect enlightenment. Like a flower in empty space, it depends on space to have its marks; when the flower in space is gone, space itself is never moved. Illusion is born of the various enlightenments; when illusion is gone, enlightenment is complete, for the mind of enlightenment is unmoved. Therefore all bodhisattvas, and all beings of the final age, should constantly depart from illusion, and all illusions will be wholly departed from. As fire comes forth from wood, and when the wood is consumed the fire dies, so enlightenment knows no gradual stages, and skillful means are just the same.”
(for annotation see
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment Explained, a Detailed Commentary

This section uses the five eyes to show that the Buddha's vision is perfectly fused, beholding all things equally, and, amid what appears to be birth and death, seeing only the unborn. Hence its title, One-Vessel Contemplation.
[Subhuti! What do you think? Does the Tathagata have the physical eye? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the physical eye.]
The Buddha asked Subhuti: What do you think? Does the Tathagata have the physical eye? Subhuti answered: So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the physical eye.
[The physical eye] The physical eye is the eye of an ordinary being of flesh and blood; when it meets darkness or an obstacle, it cannot see.
[Subhuti! What do you think? Does the Tathagata have the divine eye? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the divine eye.]
The Buddha asked Subhuti: What do you think? Does the Tathagata have the divine eye? Subhuti answered: So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the divine eye.
[The divine eye] The divine eye is the eye of the gods; near and far, by day and by night, it can see all.
[Subhuti! What do you think? Does the Tathagata have the wisdom eye? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the wisdom eye.]
The Buddha asked Subhuti: What do you think? Does the Tathagata have the wisdom eye? Subhuti answered: So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the wisdom eye.

[The wisdom eye] The wisdom eye is the eye of the shravaka; it can see through false marks and recognize true emptiness. [True emptiness] The state beyond all marks of form and consciousness—that is, the nirvāṇa of the Lesser Vehicle.
[Subhuti! What do you think? Does the Tathagata have the Dharma eye? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the Dharma eye.]
The Buddha asked Subhuti: What do you think? Does the Tathagata have the Dharma eye? Subhuti answered: So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the Dharma eye.
[The Dharma eye] The Dharma eye is the eye of the bodhisattva; it can thoroughly comprehend every Dharma gate within and beyond the world.
[Subhuti! What do you think? Does the Tathagata have the Buddha eye? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the Buddha eye.]
The Buddha asked Subhuti: What do you think? Does the Tathagata have the Buddha eye? Subhuti answered: So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the Buddha eye.

[The Buddha eye] The Buddha eye is the eye of the Tathagata; having the Buddha eye, one also possesses the four preceding eyes. Nothing is unknown, nothing is unseen; within all dharmas the Buddha eye constantly illumines.

The next passage says that the Tathagata has these five eyes (the physical eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye), knowing all and seeing all, and therefore whatever the Tathagata speaks is true speech seen with his own eyes.

[Subhuti, what do you think? Of all the sand in the Ganges River, would the Buddha say that it is sand? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata says that it is sand. Subhuti! What do you think? If there were as many Ganges Rivers as the grains of sand in one Ganges River, and the Buddha-worlds were as many as the grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers, would that not be many? Very many, World-Honored One! The Buddha told Subhuti: Within all those lands, the various minds of all the beings—the Tathagata knows them all.]

The Buddha asked Subhuti: What do you think? Of all the sand in the Ganges River, would the Buddha say that it is sand? Subhuti answered: So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata says that it is sand. The Buddha asked Subhuti: What do you think? If all the sand in the Ganges River—one grain of sand for one Ganges River—made Buddha-worlds as numerous as the grains of sand of all those Ganges Rivers, would that not be many? Subhuti answered: Very many, World-Honored One! The Buddha told Subhuti: Within all those lands of yours (that is, within the three thousand great thousand worlds multiplied by the sands of the Ganges and multiplied again by the sands of the Ganges), all the various minds (thoughts) of all beings—the Tathagata knows them all completely.

[Mind] The “mind” here means the deluded mind, that is, thoughts. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “All beings, from beginningless time, have had all manner of inversions, like a confused person who mistakes the four directions and changes his place; they falsely take the four great elements as the mark of their own bodies, and the shadowy traces of the six dusts as the mark of their own minds.” [The shadowy traces of the six dusts] These are the images that arise in dependence on the six dusts, that is, the thoughts that arise when the six faculties meet the six dusts. [Within all those lands of yours] This refers to “as many Ganges Rivers as the grains of sand in one Ganges River, and the Buddha-worlds as numerous as the grains of sand of all those Ganges Rivers”; that is, the three thousand great thousand worlds multiplied by the sands of the Ganges and multiplied again by the sands of the Ganges.
[Why is that? The Tathagata says that all minds are not minds, and so they are called minds.]

Why is it that the Tathagata knows all these countless minds completely? Because the Tathagata says that all minds (marks that exist) are not minds (their substance being nonexistent), and so they are called minds (they are illusion).

[All minds] That is, what the passage above calls “the various minds of all beings.” [The Tathagata says that all minds are not minds, and so they are called minds] This says that the minds of all beings are illusions. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra,

Chapter Eleven, on the Illusion-Like, says: “Subhuti, what do you think? Is form different from an illusion? Are feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness different from an illusion? Subhuti said: No, World-Honored One.” Thus we know that body and mind are illusions.

This passage says: Why does the Tathagata know all these countless minds? Because they are the deluded mind of thought-streaming, they are illusions, and illusions have marks (modern science and technology can already measure and record the brain waves produced by thinking), and therefore the Tathagata knows them all.

When an ordinary being gives rise to a thought, the ghosts and spirits all know it—how much more so the Tathagata. In the reign of Emperor Suzong of the Tang, a bhikshu came from the West, known as the Great-Eared Tripiṭaka, who claimed to have the power of knowing others' minds (the supernatural power of knowing the thoughts of others). Suzong asked National Master Huizhong of Nanyang to test him. The National Master sat for a while and asked: Where is this old monk's mind? He answered: Watching a boat race in Sichuan. After a while the National Master asked again: Where is this old monk's mind? He answered: Watching a monkey show on the Tianjin Bridge. The National Master became utterly still. After a while he asked again: Where is this old monk's mind? The Great-Eared Tripiṭaka could not answer for a very long time, because the National Master's mind had come to rest, still and without marks.
[What is the reason? Subhuti! The past mind cannot be grasped, the present mind cannot be grasped, the future mind cannot be grasped.]

Why is it said that (these minds) are illusions? Because the past mind, the present mind, and the future mind are all shadowy traces of the six dusts, arising from the dusts and ceasing when the dusts depart (they cannot be grasped); therefore no substance can be spoken of.

The Sutra of the Great Vehicle's Contemplation of the Mind-ground of the Original Birth says: “All mental dharmas of the three times are by nature empty.” The three minds are what dwells; the six dusts are what is dwelt upon; what dwells and what is dwelt upon are both illusions and both cannot be grasped. Therefore one must certainly see through and let go—see through the fact that all marks whatsoever are false and vain, and let go of clinging, discrimination, and false thinking.
[The three times] Past, present, and future.

blocks.text: Universal Transformation of the Dharma Realm, Chapter Nineteen

inline.s: The passage above says that the three minds are illusion; this section says that merit is illusion. “Universal transformation of the Dharma realm” means: if one realizes that merit is an illusion and practices giving without marks, one's giving and transformation pervade the Dharma realm. This is exactly what is said in Section Four, “Wondrous Practice without Dwelling”: “Subhuti! What do you think? Can the space in the east be measured? No, World-Honored One. Subhuti! Can the space in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above and below, be measured? No, World-Honored One. Subhuti! When a bodhisattva gives without dwelling in marks, the merit is likewise inconceivable and immeasurable.”

[Subhuti! What do you think? If someone filled the three thousand great thousand worlds with the seven treasures and used them for giving, would this person, by this causal condition, obtain much merit? So it is, World-Honored One! This person, by this causal condition, obtains very much merit.]

Subhuti! What do you think? If someone took the seven treasures filling the three thousand great thousand worlds and used them for giving, would this person, by this causal condition, obtain much merit? Subhuti answered: So it is, World-Honored One! This person, by this causal condition, obtains very much merit.
[Subhuti! If merit had reality, the Tathagata would not say that much merit is obtained; because merit is without reality, the Tathagata says that much merit is obtained.]

Subhuti! If merit had reality (truly existed), the Tathagata would not say that much merit is obtained; because merit is without reality (it does not truly exist), the Tathagata says that much merit is obtained.

The World-Honored One explains once more: only because merit is illusion is there any “much” to speak of. Compare Section Eight: “Subhuti! What do you think? If a person filled the three thousand great thousand worlds with the seven treasures and used them for giving, would the merit obtained by this person be much? Subhuti said: Very much, World-Honored One! Why? Because this merit is not the nature of merit; therefore the Tathagata says that the merit is much.” In Section Eight it is Subhuti who says that only because merit is illusion is there any “much” to speak of; here it is the World-Honored One who says that only because merit is illusion is there any “much” to speak of.

blocks.text: Free of Form, Free of Marks, Chapter Twenty

inline.s: This section says that the Buddha's perfect body of form is illusion, and that the Buddha's thirty-two major marks of a great being and eighty auspicious characteristics are likewise illusion. “Free of form, free of marks” means that the Buddha's perfect body of form, his thirty-two major marks of a great being, and his eighty auspicious characteristics must not be taken as real.

[Subhuti! What do you think? Can the Buddha be seen by his perfect body of form? No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata should not be seen by his perfect body of form. Why? The Tathagata says that the perfect body of form is not the perfect body of form, and so it is called the perfect body of form.]

Subhuti! What do you think? Can the Buddha be seen by his perfect body of form? Subhuti answered: No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata should not be seen by his perfect body of form. Why? Because the perfect body of form is an illusion—the Tathagata says that the perfect body of form (a mark that exists) is not the perfect body of form (its substance being nonexistent), and so it is called the perfect body of form (it is illusion).
[The perfect body of form] The perfect body of form.

The perfect body of form has marks, and all marks whatsoever are false and vain; therefore the Tathagata cannot be seen by it. The sutra says: “If you see that all marks are non-marks, then you see the Tathagata.”

[Subhuti! What do you think? Can the Tathagata be seen by his perfect marks? No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata should not be seen by his perfect marks. Why? The Tathagata says that the perfection of marks is not perfection, and so it is called the perfection of marks.]

Subhuti! What do you think? Can the Buddha be seen by his perfect marks? Subhuti answered: No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata should not be seen by his perfect marks. Why? Because this very perfection is also an illusion—the Tathagata says that the perfection of marks (a mark that exists) is not perfection (its substance being nonexistent), and so it is called the perfection of marks (it is illusion).

[The perfect marks] The thirty-two major marks of a great being and the eighty auspicious characteristics with which the Buddha's body of form is endowed. Among the supremely excellent features and forms of the Buddha's body of form, those that are prominent and easily seen are thirty-two in number, called the thirty-two major marks of a great being (the thirty-two marks for short); those that are subtle, hidden, and hard to see are eighty in number, called the eighty auspicious characteristics. A wheel-turning sage king also possesses the thirty-two marks, but does not possess the eighty characteristics.

The thirty-two major marks of a great being and the eighty auspicious characteristics” have marks, and all marks whatsoever are false and vain; therefore the Tathagata cannot be seen by them. The sutra says: “If you see that all marks are non-marks, then you see the Tathagata.”

Compare: Section Five, “The Real Seeing of Suchness”: “Subhuti! What do you think? Can the Tathagata be seen by his bodily marks? No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata cannot be seen by his bodily marks. Why? The bodily marks spoken of by the Tathagata are not bodily marks.” Section Thirteen, “Upholding the Dharma as Taught”: “Subhuti, what do you think? Can the Tathagata be seen by the thirty-two marks? No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata cannot be seen by the thirty-two marks. Why? The Tathagata says that the thirty-two marks are not marks, and so they are called the thirty-two marks.”

blocks.text: Neither Speaking Nor What Is Spoken, Chapter Twenty-One

inline.s: “Neither speaking nor what is spoken”—one who speaks the Dharma has no dharma to speak, and so is called speaking the Dharma.

[Subhuti! Do not say that the Tathagata has this thought: I should speak some Dharma. Do not have this thought! Why? If a person says that the Tathagata speaks a Dharma, he slanders the Buddha, because he cannot understand what I have spoken.]

Subhuti! Do not think that the Tathagata has this thought: I should speak some Dharma. Do not think so! Why? If a person says that the Tathagata has the thought that he speaks the Dharma, that is slandering the Buddha, because this person cannot understand what my speaking of the Dharma really is. (The Buddha speaks while free of marks—speaking yet not speaking.)

The Tathagata's speaking of the Dharma is not speaking from a thought (the Tathagata has no thought of wanting to speak the Dharma, nor any thought of being about to speak or having already spoken the Dharma); rather, it responds to conditions and arises in function, flowing naturally from the self-nature. The Tathagata does not cling to the mark of speaking the Dharma—speaking yet not speaking, as is said: “How does one expound it for others? Not grasping at marks, abiding in unmoved suchness.” (See Section Thirty-Two, “Neither Real nor Illusory.”) Moreover, this very matter of the Tathagata's speaking the Dharma is not truly existent; truly there is no dharma called speaking the Dharma. (For “the Tathagata has spoken nothing,” see Section Thirteen, “Upholding the Dharma as Taught”: “Subhuti! What do you think? Has the Tathagata spoken any Dharma? Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! The Tathagata has spoken nothing.”)
[Subhuti! One who speaks the Dharma has no dharma to speak, and so is called speaking the Dharma.]
Subhuti! One who speaks the Dharma has no dharma to speak—this alone is truly speaking the Dharma.

The meaning is that one who clings to the mark of speaking the Dharma (the conditioned Dharma) cannot speak the way of liberation (the unconditioned Dharma), because he himself has not realized and has not upheld the way of liberation. Therefore, at the end of this sutra, the World-Honored One admonishes: “How does one expound it for others? Not grasping at marks, abiding in unmoved suchness.” (Section Thirty-Two, “Neither Real nor Illusory.”) At the same time, the self-nature of beings is originally perfect and complete, no different from the Buddhas; in this respect there truly is no dharma to speak, no practice to cultivate, and no fruit to realize. The problem is that the Buddhas are awake and have verified their own nature, while we are still within the dream of delusion and must cultivate and realize before we can awaken. In this respect there is a dharma that must be spoken, a practice that must be cultivated, and a fruit that must be realized. Yet these dharmas, practices, and fruits are all carried on within the dream of ignorance; though it is using illusion to depart from illusion, after all they are illusions, and illusions are not real. The practitioner must never cling to marks. Therefore it is said: no dharma to speak, no practice to cultivate, no fruit to realize.

Master Hanshan says: Beings “only because of beginningless ignorance, which obscures for them the wondrous brightness, give rise to all manner of inversion, false thinking, and discrimination, and create all manner of karma. It is like a waking person who, having nothing to do, suddenly in sleep dreams all manner of dreams; the affairs of joy and sorrow in the dream appear vividly before him, yet when he wakes and looks for them, they cannot be found at all. This is what is called producing something out of nothing—how could it be a real dharma? But the deluded person, being inverted, clings to it as truly existent; this is because his seeing is not thorough. And when the Buddha comes into the world and speaks all manner of dharmas, these are but tools for breaking the dream, and have no root either. Yet students of the Buddha-Dharma again cling to them as dharmas that they truly possess—this is adding a dream within a dream.” (The Dream Wandering Collection
Shown to the Chan Practitioner Tanyan Zong)

The Essential Sayings of the Transmission of the Mind says: “The Buddha has three bodies: the Dharma body speaks the Dharma of the self-nature's empty pervasion, the reward body speaks all pure dharmas, and the transformation body speaks the Dharma of the six perfections and the myriad practices. When the Dharma body speaks the Dharma, it cannot be sought by speech, sound, form, or letters; there is nothing spoken and nothing realized, only the self-nature's empty pervasion. Hence it is said: ‘No dharma to speak—this is called speaking the Dharma.’ The reward body and the transformation body both appear in response to the capacities of beings, and the dharmas they speak also follow the matter and respond to the faculties so as to gather and transform them; none of these are the true Dharma. Hence it is said: the reward and transformation bodies are not the true Buddha, nor are they speakers of the Dharma.”

Master Baojing says: “Now the mark of the stillness and extinction of all dharmas cannot be proclaimed in words; in the ground of actual principle there is originally nothing spoken. This is what is meant by ‘the Way is originally without words, the Dharma is originally without speech.’ As the Diamond Sutra says: if one says that the Tathagata has spoken a Dharma, that is slandering the Buddha. Why then does the Buddha have a Dharma that can be spoken? You should know that the Way is originally without words, and words are borrowed to reveal the Way; the Dharma is originally without speech, and speech is used to reveal the Dharma. If one clings to its being un-speakable, one falls into the outsider's view of cutting off words; if one clings to there being something speakable, one earns the reproach of slandering the Buddha. If one understands that speaking is precisely not speaking, then one may well speak without speaking. Therefore the World-Honored One taught the Dharma for forty-nine years and never spoke a single word. Yet though he never spoke a single word, he spoke horizontally and vertically, speaking ardently and without interval, without end. The wonder of the Buddha-Dharma lies precisely in this.” (A Personal Record of the Essential Explanation of the Amitabha Sutra)
[At that time the life-of-wisdom Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! Will there be many beings in future ages who, hearing this Dharma, give rise to faith?]
At that time the life-of-wisdom Subhuti reverently said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! Many beings in future ages, hearing you speak in this way, will they believe it?
[Life of wisdom] To take wisdom as one's life. Subhuti was foremost in understanding emptiness, taking wisdom as his life, and so he is called the life-of-wisdom Subhuti.

The passage above says: “If a person says that the Tathagata speaks a Dharma, he slanders the Buddha . . . one who speaks the Dharma has no dharma to speak, and so is called speaking the Dharma.” Subhuti feared that beings would find this hard to understand, and so asked: in future ages, hearing you speak in this way, will any beings believe it?
[The Buddha said: Subhuti! They are not beings, and yet they are not non-beings. Why? Subhuti! Beings, beings, the Tathagata says are not beings, and so they are called beings.]
